_note: Teaching content (PRD v2 §8 ContentItem). Every claim is general information, not legal advice, and carries its official source. verified_by records who checked it; the PRD asks for teammate initials, so items checked only by the AI assistant are flagged for a teammate to re-check.

items.claim: A big red flag: the rent is much lower than similar places nearby.
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: Rental scam: no room for error
items.short: Red flag: rent much lower than similar places nearby.

items.claim: Scammers often claim to be abroad and unable to show you inside the place.
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: Rental scam: no room for error
items.short: Red flag: the "owner" is abroad and can't show you inside.

items.claim: Being asked to leave a deposit without any formal rental agreement or lease in place is a warning sign.
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: Rental scam: no room for error
items.short: Red flag: a deposit asked for before any lease or rental agreement.

items.claim: Watch out for being sent to a website that asks for personal or financial information.
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: Rental scam: no room for error
items.short: Red flag: a website asking for your personal or financial information.

items.claim: Suspected rental fraud can be reported to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre (1-888-495-8501) or to police.
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: Rental scam: no room for error
items.short: Report rental fraud to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre or police.

items.claim: If you already sent money, notify the financial institution you sent it to and tell them you are reporting fraudulent activity.
items.contact: The bank, credit union, or payment service that moved the money
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: How to report fraud and scams in Canada
items.short: Tell the bank you sent the money to that it was fraud.

items.claim: Keep the listing, messages, screenshots and transfer receipts. Hold onto them in case police or the bank ask.
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: How to report fraud and scams in Canada
items.short: Save the ad, the messages and the transfer receipt.

items.claim: If you lost money, report the fraud to your local police and keep the file number they give you.
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: How to report fraud and scams in Canada
items.short: Lost money? Report it to local police and keep the file number.

items.claim: If you shared banking or identity details, ask Equifax Canada and TransUnion Canada to put a fraud alert on your credit file.
items.source_title: Competition Bureau Canada: How to report fraud and scams in Canada
items.short: Shared banking info? Ask both credit bureaus for a fraud alert.

items.claim: When viewing, look for mould and water damage: stains on walls, musty smells or rotting wood.
items.source_title: CMHC: Visiting the rental property
items.short: Look for water damage: stains, musty smells or rotting wood.

items.claim: Check for working smoke detectors. In Toronto, landlords must install smoke alarms and keep them working.
items.source_title: City of Toronto: Smoke alarms
items.short: In Toronto, landlords must install smoke alarms and keep them working.

items.claim: Check the locks on windows and doors, and ask the landlord to change them at their expense before you move in.
items.source_title: CMHC: Visiting the rental property
items.short: Check locks; ask the landlord to change them, at their expense, before move-in.

items.claim: Pests are something to raise with the landlord, in writing, before they become your problem.
items.source_title: City of Toronto: RentSafeTO for tenants: service requests
items.short: Raise pests with the landlord, in writing, before they're your problem.

items.claim: Ask whether heat, electricity, water and internet are included, and whether parking, storage or laundry cost extra.
items.source_title: CMHC: Visiting the rental property
items.short: Ask what's included: heat, hydro, water, internet, parking, storage, laundry.

items.claim: Landlords may ask for rental history, credit references and/or a credit check, and about your income alongside them.
items.source_title: Ontario Human Rights Commission: Human rights for tenants
items.short: Landlords may ask for rental history, credit references or checks, and income alongside them.

items.claim: A lack of rental or credit history should not count against you, and a rent-to-income cut-off is not allowed outside subsidized housing.
items.source_title: Ontario Human Rights Commission: Human rights for tenants
items.short: No credit history shouldn't count against you; rent-to-income cut-offs aren't allowed outside subsidized housing.

items.claim: A rent deposit is limited to one month's rent for monthly tenants, and can only be used as rent for the last month.
items.source_title: Landlord and Tenant Board: A Guide to the Residential Tenancies Act
items.short: Monthly tenants: rent deposit is at most one month's rent, used for your last month.

items.claim: Most Ontario leases signed since April 30, 2018 must use the standard lease, and the landlord must give you a copy within 21 days of signing.
items.source_title: Government of Ontario: Guide to Ontario's standard lease
items.short: Most Ontario leases signed since April 30, 2018 must use the standard form.

items.claim: Terms that ban pets, or ban guests, roommates or other occupants, are void and can't be enforced.
items.source_title: Government of Ontario: Guide to Ontario's standard lease
items.short: Lease terms banning pets, guests, roommates or other occupants are void.

items.claim: Terms requiring deposits, fees or penalties the law doesn't allow, such as damage or pet deposits, are void. A rent deposit can't be used as a damage deposit.
items.source_title: Government of Ontario: Guide to Ontario's standard lease
items.short: Terms requiring fees the law doesn't allow, like damage or pet deposits, are void.

items.claim: A term making the tenant pay for repairs the landlord is responsible for is void. Landlords must keep the property in a good state of repair.
items.source_title: Government of Ontario: Guide to Ontario's standard lease
items.short: Making you pay for repairs the landlord is responsible for is a void term.

items.claim: For most reasons, a landlord must give 24 hours' written notice before entering, with the reason and a time between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.
items.source_title: Landlord and Tenant Board: A Guide to the Residential Tenancies Act
items.short: For most reasons, landlords need 24 hours' written notice and an 8 a.m.–8 p.m. time.

items.claim: A lease can require tenant liability insurance; contents insurance for your own belongings is up to you.
items.source_title: Government of Ontario: Guide to Ontario's standard lease
items.short: A lease can require liability insurance; contents insurance is your choice.

items.claim: Document the unit's condition on moving day, ideally together with the landlord. Photograph any problems and keep a back-up.
items.source_title: CMHC: Inspections
items.short: On move-in day, photograph any problems and keep a back-up.

items.claim: Talk to your landlord first, make repair requests in writing and keep a copy. Landlords must respond to urgent requests within 24 hours and non-urgent ones within seven days. If it isn't resolved, contact 311.
items.source_title: City of Toronto: RentSafeTO for tenants: service requests
items.short: Ask the landlord in writing and keep a copy; if unresolved, call 311.

items.claim: A City bylaw requires landlords to keep rental units at least 21°C from October 1 to May 15 where the owner pays for heat. Tell your landlord first; if it isn't fixed, call 311.
items.source_title: City of Toronto: Indoor temperatures in apartment units
items.short: Landlord-heated units must stay at least 21°C, October 1 to May 15.

items.claim: Tell your landlord as soon as a smoke alarm stops working. If they don't fix it, call 311 for a referral to Toronto Fire Services.
items.source_title: City of Toronto: Smoke alarms
items.short: Broken smoke alarm? Tell your landlord; if they don't fix it, call 311.

items.claim: Rent can generally go up once every 12 months with at least 90 days' written notice, by no more than the guideline (2.1% for 2026). Units first occupied after November 15, 2018 are exempt from rent control.
items.source_title: Government of Ontario: Residential rent increases
items.short: Most rent increases: 12 months apart, 90 days' written notice, max 2.1% in 2026.

items.claim: If a landlord isn't meeting their maintenance obligations, a tenant can apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board.
items.source_title: Landlord and Tenant Board: A Guide to the Residential Tenancies Act
items.short: If maintenance obligations aren't met, tenants can apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board.

items.claim: The TTC is a City of Toronto agency, and its Board-approved service standards guide how often routes run and what counts as an on-time departure.
items.source_title: TTC report: Overview of TTC Service Standards (September 4, 2025)
items.short: TTC service standards, set through a City agency, guide frequency and on-time targets.

items.claim: To end a monthly tenancy you must give at least 60 days' written notice (Form N9), ending on the last day of a rental month.
items.source_title: Landlord and Tenant Board: How a Tenant Can End Their Tenancy
items.short: Monthly tenancy: at least 60 days' written notice on Form N9, ending a rental month.

items.claim: Your rent deposit covers your last month's rent, and the landlord must pay you interest on it every year. It can't be kept as a damage deposit.
items.source_title: Landlord and Tenant Board: A Guide to the Residential Tenancies Act
items.short: Your rent deposit covers your last month, plus yearly interest; it's not a damage deposit.
